ch3.desc: Write is_even(n) that returns True if n % 2 == 0 else False. Print is_even(8) and is_even(7).
ch3.code: def is_even(n): return n % 2 == 0 print(is_even(8), is_even(7))
guidance: Return the result of a boolean expression.
8 % 2 == 0 is True; 7 % 2 == 0 is False.

ch3.title: Define and Call with One Argument
ch3.desc: Define triple(x) that returns 3 * x. Call triple(5) and print the result.
ch3.code: def triple(x): return 3 * x print(triple(___)) # 15
guidance: One parameter x; one argument 5 when you call triple(5).
Fill: 5.

ch3.title: Arguments in Call
ch3.desc: Given def greet(first, last): print(first, last), call it so it prints 'Jane Doe'.
ch3.code: def greet(first, last): print(first, last) greet(___, ___)
guidance: Pass two arguments in order: first then last.
Fill: "Jane", "Doe" (or 'Jane', 'Doe').

ch3.title: Multiple Return (tuple)
ch3.desc: Write min_max(a, b) that returns the smaller and larger as a tuple. Print min_max(10, 3).
ch3.code: def min_max(a, b): if a < b: return (a, b) return (b, a) print(min_max(10, 3)) # (3, 10)
guidance: You can return one tuple: return (a, b).
Return (b, a) when b is smaller so order is (min, max).

ch3.title: Keyword Arguments
ch3.desc: Define greet(greeting, name) and call it using keyword arguments: name='Sam', greeting='Hi'.
ch3.code: def greet(greeting, name): print(greeting + " " + name) greet(name="Sam", greeting="Hi")
guidance: Keyword args: greet(name="Sam", greeting="Hi") — order does not matter.
Output: Hi Sam.

ch3.title: Positional vs Keyword
ch3.desc: Define f(a, b, c). Call f(1, 2, 3) then f(1, c=3, b=2). Both should give the same result.
ch3.code: def f(a, b, c): return a + b + c print(f(1, 2, 3), f(1, ___=3, b=2)) # 6 6
guidance: Positional: order matters. Keyword: name=value.
Fill: c so f(1, c=3, b=2) is 6.

ch3.title: *args
ch3.desc: Define sum_all(*args) that returns the sum of all positional arguments. sum_all(1, 2, 3) → 6.
ch3.code: def sum_all(*args): total = 0 for n in args: total += n return total print(sum_all(1, 2, 3))
guidance: *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple.
Loop over args and add to total.

ch3.title: **kwargs
ch3.desc: Define print_kw(**kwargs) that prints each key and value. Call print_kw(a=1, b=2).
ch3.code: def print_kw(**kwargs): for k, v in kwargs.items(): print(k, v) print_kw(a=1, b=2)
guidance: **kwargs collects keyword arguments into a dict.
kwargs.items() gives (key, value) pairs.

ch3.title: *args and **kwargs
ch3.desc: Define f(*args, **kwargs) that returns (len(args), len(kwargs)). Print f(1, 2, x=3).
ch3.code: def f(*args, **kwargs): return (len(args), len(kwargs)) print(f(1, 2, x=3)) # (2, 1)
guidance: *args gets (1, 2); **kwargs gets {"x": 3}.
len(args)==2, len(kwargs)==1.

ch3.title: Default and Keyword
ch3.desc: Define greet(name, greeting='Hello'). Call greet('A') then greet('B', greeting='Hi').
ch3.code: def greet(name, greeting="Hello"): print(greeting, name) greet("A") greet("B", greeting="Hi")
guidance: Default: greet("A") uses greeting='Hello'.
Keyword overrides: greet("B", greeting="Hi").

ch3.title: Decorator Basics
ch3.desc: Write a decorator log that prints 'calling' before invoking the function. Apply it to def hi(): print('hi').
ch3.code: def log(fn): def wrapper(): print("calling") return fn() return wrapper @log def hi(): print("hi") hi()
guidance: Decorator takes a function and returns a wrapper.
@log applies log to hi; calling hi() runs wrapper, which prints then fn().

ch3.title: Decorator with Wrapper
ch3.desc: Write a decorator that doubles the return value of a function. Apply it to def two(): return 2 and print the result.
ch3.code: def double_ret(fn): def wrapper(): return fn() * 2 return wrapper @double_ret def two(): return 2 print(two()) # 4
guidance: Wrapper calls fn() and returns twice that value.
two() returns 2; decorator makes it return 4.

ch3.title: Lambda: Add
ch3.desc: Create a lambda that adds 10 to its argument. Assign to add_10; print add_10(5) → 15.
ch3.code: add_10 = lambda x: x + 10 print(add_10(5)) # 15
guidance: lambda x: x + 10 is an anonymous function.
add_10(5) returns 15. Fill: 5.

ch3.title: Lambda: Double
ch3.desc: Create lambda double that multiplies its argument by 2. Print double(7).
ch3.code: double = lambda x: x * 2 print(double(7)) # 14
guidance: lambda x: x * 2.
double(7) is 14. Fill: 2.

ch3.title: Lambda: Compare
ch3.desc: Create lambda is_positive that returns True if x > 0 else False. Print is_positive(5) and is_positive(-1).
ch3.code: is_positive = lambda x: x ___ 0 print(is_positive(5), is_positive(-1)) # True False
guidance: lambda x: x > 0 returns a boolean.
Fill: > (greater than).

ch3.title: Lambda: Multi-arg
ch3.desc: Lambda can take multiple parameters: area = lambda w, h: w * h. Print area(3, 4).
ch3.code: area = lambda w, h: w * h print(area(3, 4)) # 12
guidance: lambda w, h: w * h takes two arguments.
area(3, 4) is 12.

ch3.title: Keyword-Only (after *)
ch3.desc: Define f(a, *, b) so b must be passed by keyword. Call f(1, b=2) and print a + b.
ch3.code: def f(a, *, b): return a + b print(f(1, b=2)) # 3
guidance: After *, parameters are keyword-only.
f(1, b=2) is valid; f(1, 2) would be invalid. Fill: 2.

ch3.title: Unpack List to *args
ch3.desc: Define add3(a,b,c) return a+b+c. Given nums = [1,2,3], call add3 with unpacking: add3(*nums).
ch3.code: def add3(a, b, c): return a + b + c nums = [1, 2, 3] print(add3(*nums)) # 6
guidance: *nums unpacks the list into three positional arguments.

ch3.title: Unpack Dict to **kwargs
ch3.desc: Define greet(greeting, name). Given d = {'greeting':'Hi','name':'Jo'}, call greet(**d).
ch3.code: def greet(greeting, name): print(greeting, name) d = {"greeting": "Hi", "name": "Jo"} greet(**d)
guidance: **d unpacks the dict as keyword arguments.
greet(**d) is greet(greeting='Hi', name='Jo').

ch3.title: Return Multiple Unpack
ch3.desc: Write get_pair() that returns (10, 20). Call it and unpack into x, y; print x + y.
ch3.code: def get_pair(): return (10, 20) x, y = get_pair() print(x + y) # 30
guidance: Return a tuple; assign with unpacking: x, y = get_pair().

ch3.title: Function as Object
ch3.desc: Assign a function to a variable: f = abs. Then call f(-5) and print the result.
ch3.code: f = abs print(f(-5)) # 5
guidance: In Python, functions are objects. f = abs; then f(-5) is abs(-5).
Fill: -5.

ch3.title: Decorator with Args
ch3.desc: Write repeat(n) that returns a decorator which runs the function n times and returns the last result. Use @repeat(2) on def one(): return 1; print one() → 1.
ch3.code: def repeat(n): def dec(fn): def wrapper(): out = None for _ in range(n): out = fn() return out return wrapper return dec @repeat(2) def one(): return 1 print(one())
guidance: repeat(n) returns a decorator dec. dec(fn) returns wrapper that calls fn() n times.
Return the last result. one() is called twice, returns 1.

ch3.title: Lambda in sorted
ch3.desc: Sort [(1,2), (3,1), (2,3)] by the second element using key=lambda t: t[1]. Print result.
ch3.code: pairs = [(1, 2), (3, 1), (2, 3)] print(sorted(pairs, key=lambda t: t[1])) # [(3,1), (1,2), (2,3)]
guidance: key=lambda t: t[1] uses the second element of each tuple for comparison.

ch3.title: Decorator: Print Before and After
ch3.desc: Write a decorator that prints 'start' before calling the function and 'end' after. Apply it to a function that prints 'run'.
ch3.code: def trace(fn): def wrapper(): print("start") fn() print("end") return wrapper @trace def run(): print("run") run()
guidance: Call fn() in the middle of the wrapper; print before and after.
Output: start, run, end.

ch3.title: Decorator: Wrapper with Arguments
ch3.desc: Write a decorator for a function that takes one argument. The wrapper should pass the argument through: def add_one(x): return x+1; @deco; add_one(5) → 6.
ch3.code: def pass_through(fn): def wrapper(x): return fn(x) return wrapper @pass_through def add_one(x): return x + 1 print(add_one(5)) # 6
guidance: Wrapper must accept the same arguments as the wrapped function.
wrapper(x) receives 5, calls fn(5), returns 6.

ch3.title: Decorator: Caching (Memoization)
ch3.desc: Write a simple cache decorator: store results in a dict keyed by argument. On repeat call with same arg, return cached value. Apply to def slow(n): return n*2; print slow(3), slow(3).
ch3.code: def cache(fn): saved = {} def wrapper(x): if x not in saved: saved[x] = fn(x) return saved[x] return wrapper @cache def slow(n): return n * 2 print(slow(3), slow(3)) # 6 6
guidance: Use a dict in the closure to store fn(x) by x.
First slow(3) calls fn(3) and stores 6; second slow(3) returns saved[3] without calling fn.

ch3.title: Nested Function: Define and Call
ch3.desc: Define outer() that contains an inner function inner() which returns 42. outer() should call inner() and return its result. Print outer().
ch3.code: def outer(): def inner(): return 42 return inner() print(outer()) # 42
guidance: You can define a function inside another function.
inner() is only visible inside outer. outer() calls inner() and returns 42.

ch3.title: Nested Function: Access Enclosing Variable
ch3.desc: Define outer(x) with a nested inner() that returns x + 1. outer should call inner and return the result. Print outer(10).
ch3.code: def outer(x): def inner(): return x + 1 return inner() print(outer(10)) # 11
guidance: inner can read the enclosing scope: it sees x from outer.
outer(10) calls inner(), which returns 10 + 1 = 11.

ch3.title: Nested Function: Return Inner Function
ch3.desc: Define outer(prefix) with nested greet(name) that returns prefix + ' ' + name. outer should return the greet function (not call it). Then f = outer('Hi'); print f('Ali').
ch3.code: def outer(prefix): def greet(name): return prefix + " " + name return greet f = outer("Hi") print(f("Ali")) # Hi Ali
guidance: Return the inner function without calling it: return greet.
f = outer('Hi') gives f the greet that remembers prefix='Hi'. f('Ali') returns 'Hi Ali'.

ch3.title: Local Scope
ch3.desc: Inside a function, assign x = 10 and print x. Outside, print x (will error unless global).
ch3.code: def set_x(): x = 10 print(x) set_x() print(x) # NameError
guidance: Variables assigned inside a function are local.
x exists only inside set_x(). Outside, x is not defined.

ch3.title: Local vs Global
ch3.desc: Global count = 0. Function increment() has local_count = 1. Return count + local_count.
ch3.code: count = 0 def increment(): local_count = 1 return count + local_count print(increment()) # 1
guidance: Global count is visible inside. Local local_count only in function.
Return 0 + 1 = 1.

ch3.title: global Keyword
ch3.desc: Use global to modify a variable from inside a function. Set total = 0; in add(n) do global total; total += n. Call add(5), add(3), print total.
ch3.code: total = 0 def add(n): global total total += n add(5) add(3) print(total) # 8
guidance: global total says 'use the global total', not create a local.
After add(5) and add(3), total is 8.

ch3.title: Same Name Local Shadows
ch3.desc: Global x = 1. Define f() with local x = 2; print x inside f (prints 2). Print x after f (still 1).
ch3.code: x = 1 def f(): x = 2 print(x) f() print(x) # 2 then 1
guidance: Local x = 2 shadows the global x inside f.
Outside f, global x is still 1.

ch3.title: LEGB: Built-in
ch3.desc: Inside a function, print(len([1,2,3])). len is found in built-in scope. What does it print?
ch3.code: def demo(): print(len([1, 2, 3])) demo() # 3
guidance: LEGB: Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in. len is built-in.
Output: 3.

ch3.title: Enclosing Scope
ch3.desc: Define outer() with x=10; define inner() that prints x. Call outer() which calls inner().
ch3.code: def outer(): x = 10 def inner(): print(x) inner() outer() # 10
guidance: inner looks up x; not local, so it uses enclosing (outer) scope.
x is 10 in outer, so inner prints 10.

ch3.title: Read Global Without global
ch3.desc: Global y = 5. Define get_y() that returns y (no assignment to y). Print get_y().
ch3.code: y = 5 def get_y(): return y print(get_y()) # 5
guidance: You can read a global without declaring global.
Only need global when you assign to the name.

ch3.title: Closure: make_adder
ch3.desc: Define make_adder(n) that returns a function adding n to its argument. make_adder(3)(4) → 7.
ch3.code: def make_adder(n): def adder(x): return x + n return adder print(make_adder(3)(4)) # 7
guidance: adder closes over n. make_adder(3) returns a function that adds 3.
That function(4) returns 7.

ch3.title: Closure: multiply_by
ch3.desc: Define multiply_by(k) that returns a function. The returned function multiplies its argument by k. multiply_by(5)(4) → 20.
ch3.code: def multiply_by(k): def inner(z): return z * k return inner print(multiply_by(5)(4)) # 20
guidance: inner closes over k. multiply_by(5) returns a function that multiplies by 5.
That function(4) returns 20.

ch3.title: Closure: Counter
ch3.desc: Define make_counter() that returns a function. Each call to the returned function increments and returns a count (start at 0). First call → 1, second → 2.
ch3.code: def make_counter(): count = 0 def counter(): nonlocal count count += 1 return count return counter c = make_counter() print(c(), c()) # 1 2
guidance: counter closes over count. Use nonlocal count to rebind in enclosing scope.
First c() → 1, second c() → 2.

ch3.title: Closure: Greet Prefix
ch3.desc: Define make_greeter(prefix) that returns a function. The returned function takes a name and returns prefix + ' ' + name. make_greeter('Hi')('Ali') → 'Hi Ali'.
ch3.code: def make_greeter(prefix): def greet(name): return prefix + " " + name return greet print(make_greeter("Hi")("Ali"))
guidance: greet closes over prefix. make_greeter('Hi') returns a function that prepends 'Hi '.
That function('Ali') returns 'Hi Ali'.

ch3.title: Closure: Power
ch3.desc: Define make_power(exp) that returns a function. The returned function raises its argument to exp. make_power(2)(5) → 25.
ch3.code: def make_power(exp): def power(x): return x ** exp return power print(make_power(2)(5)) # 25
guidance: power closes over exp. make_power(2) returns a function that squares.
That function(5) returns 25.

ch3.title: Generator: yield
ch3.desc: Define a generator function count_to(n) that yields 1, 2, ..., n. Print list(count_to(3)).
ch3.code: def count_to(n): i = 1 while i <= n: yield i i += 1 print(list(count_to(3))) # [1, 2, 3]
guidance: Use yield instead of return; the function becomes a generator.
list(count_to(3)) consumes the generator and gives [1, 2, 3].

ch3.title: Generator: next()
ch3.desc: Create a generator g = (x for x in range(3)). Call next(g) three times and print the values.
ch3.code: g = (x for x in range(3)) print(next(g), next(g), next(g)) # 0 1 2
guidance: (x for x in range(3)) is a generator expression.
next(g) gets the next value; after 3 values the generator is exhausted.

ch3.title: Generator: Infinite Sequence
ch3.desc: Define gen() that yields 0, 1, 2, ... forever. Get first 4 values with next() in a loop and print them.
ch3.code: def gen(): n = 0 while True: yield n n += 1 g = gen() print([next(g) for _ in range(4)]) # [0,1,2,3]
guidance: Generators are lazy; they produce values on demand.
next(g) in a loop gets 0, 1, 2, 3.

ch3.title: Generator: for Loop
ch3.desc: Define a generator that yields 'a', 'b', 'c'. Iterate with for and collect into a list; print it.
ch3.code: def letters(): yield "a" yield "b" yield "c" print([x for x in letters()])
guidance: A generator can yield multiple values one by one.
for x in letters() consumes the generator; list comp gives ['a','b','c'].

ch3.title: Generator Expression
ch3.desc: Use a generator expression (x*2 for x in range(5)) and convert to list. Print the result.
ch3.code: g = (x * 2 for x in range(5)) print(list(g)) # [0, 2, 4, 6, 8]
guidance: (expr for x in iterable) is a generator expression (parens, not brackets).
list(g) consumes it: [0, 2, 4, 6, 8].

ch3.title: List Comp: Basic
ch3.desc: Build a list of squares for 1 to 5 using list comprehension: [x**2 for x in range(1,6)]. Print it.
ch3.code: squares = [x ** 2 for x in range(1, 6)] print(squares) # [1, 4, 9, 16, 25]
guidance: [expr for x in iterable] builds a list.
range(1, 6) is 1..5; x**2 gives squares.

ch3.title: List Comp: With if
ch3.desc: Build a list of even numbers from 0 to 9: [x for x in range(10) if x%2==0]. Print it.
ch3.code: evens = [x for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0] print(evens) # [0, 2, 4, 6, 8]
guidance: Add if condition at the end to filter.
Only x where x%2==0 are included.

ch3.title: List Comp: From String
ch3.desc: Build a list of uppercase letters from 'hello': [c.upper() for c in 'hello']. Print it.
ch3.code: upper_chars = [c.upper() for c in "hello"] print(upper_chars) # [H,E,L,L,O]
guidance: Iterate over a string; each c is a character.
c.upper() gives uppercase; result ['H','E','L','L','O'].

ch3.title: List Comp: Nested
ch3.desc: Build a 2x3 matrix as list of lists: [[i*j for j in range(1,4)] for i in range(1,3)]. Print it.
ch3.code: matrix = [[i * j for j in range(1, 4)] for i in range(1, 3)] print(matrix) # [[1,2,3], [2,4,6]]
guidance: Inner comp builds a row; outer comp builds rows.

ch3.title: List Comp: With Else
ch3.desc: Build list: ['even' if n%2==0 else 'odd' for n in [1,2,3,4]]. Print it.
ch3.code: labels = ["even" if n % 2 == 0 else "odd" for n in [1, 2, 3, 4]] print(labels) # [odd, even, odd, even]
guidance: a if cond else b for x in ... uses conditional expression per item.
Result: ['odd','even','odd','even'].

ch3.title: Tuple from List Comp
ch3.desc: Build a tuple of doubles for 1..5: tuple([x*2 for x in range(1,6)]). Print it.
ch3.code: t = tuple([x * 2 for x in range(1, 6)]) print(t) # (2, 4, 6, 8, 10)
guidance: Python has no tuple comprehension syntax; use tuple([...]) from a list comp.
Or use tuple(generator_expression).

ch3.title: Tuple from Generator
ch3.desc: Build a tuple using a generator expression: tuple(x for x in range(5)). Print it.
ch3.code: t = tuple(x for x in range(5)) print(t) # (0, 1, 2, 3, 4)
guidance: tuple(gen_expr) consumes the generator and builds an immutable tuple.
tuple(x for x in range(5)) → (0,1,2,3,4).

ch3.title: Tuple Comp: Squares
ch3.desc: Build tuple of squares of 1,2,3: tuple(x**2 for x in [1,2,3]). Print it.
ch3.code: squares = tuple(x ** 2 for x in [1, 2, 3]) print(squares) # (1, 4, 9)
guidance: Generator expression inside tuple(): (x**2 for x in [1,2,3]).
Result: (1, 4, 9).

ch3.title: Tuple Comp: With if
ch3.desc: Build tuple of positive numbers from [-1, 2, -3, 4]: tuple(x for x in ... if x > 0). Print it.
ch3.code: t = tuple(x for x in [-1, 2, -3, 4] if x > 0) print(t) # (2, 4)
guidance: Filter in generator: x for x in ... if x > 0.
Only 2 and 4 are positive.

ch3.title: Tuple from String
ch3.desc: Build a tuple of characters from 'abc': tuple(c for c in 'abc'). Print it.
ch3.code: chars = tuple(c for c in "abc") print(chars) # (a, b, c)
guidance: Iterate over string; tuple() collects the characters.
Result: ('a', 'b', 'c').

ch3.title: Set Comp: Basic
ch3.desc: Build a set of squares for 1..5: {x**2 for x in range(1,6)}. Print it (order may vary).
ch3.code: s = {x ** 2 for x in range(1, 6)} print(s) # {1, 4, 9, 16, 25}
guidance: {expr for x in iterable} is set comprehension; result has no duplicates.
Sets are unordered.

ch3.title: Set Comp: With if
ch3.desc: Build set of even numbers from 0 to 9: {x for x in range(10) if x%2==0}. Print it.
ch3.code: evens = {x for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0} print(evens) # {0, 2, 4, 6, 8}
guidance: Set comp with filter: only even x.
Result: {0, 2, 4, 6, 8} (order not guaranteed).

ch3.title: Set Comp: From String
ch3.desc: Build set of unique characters in 'hello': {c for c in 'hello'}. Print it.
ch3.code: unique = {c for c in "hello"} print(unique) # {h, e, l, o}
guidance: Set automatically removes duplicates.
'hello' → {'h','e','l','o'} (4 unique chars).

ch3.title: Set Comp: Lengths
ch3.desc: Build set of lengths of words: {len(w) for w in ['a','hi','foo']}. Print it.
ch3.code: lengths = {len(w) for w in ["a", "hi", "foo"]} print(lengths) # {1, 2, 3}
guidance: Expression can be any expression; len(w) for each word.
Result: {1, 2, 3}.

ch3.title: Set Comp: Upper
ch3.desc: Build set of uppercase letters from 'abc': {c.upper() for c in 'abc'}. Print it.
ch3.code: upper_set = {c.upper() for c in "abc"} print(upper_set) # {A, B, C}
guidance: Set of transformed elements.
Result: {'A', 'B', 'C'}.

ch3.title: Dict Comp: Basic
ch3.desc: Build dict mapping 1..5 to their squares: {x: x**2 for x in range(1,6)}. Print it.
ch3.code: d = {x: x ** 2 for x in range(1, 6)} print(d) # {1:1, 2:4, 3:9, 4:16, 5:25}
guidance: {key_expr: value_expr for x in iterable} builds a dict.

ch3.title: Dict Comp: From Two Lists
ch3.desc: Build dict from keys ['a','b','c'] and values [1,2,3]: {k: v for k,v in zip(keys, values)}. Print it.
ch3.code: keys = ["a", "b", "c"] vals = [1, 2, 3] d = {k: v for k, v in zip(keys, vals)} print(d)
guidance: zip(keys, vals) gives (a,1), (b,2), (c,3).
Dict comp: {k: v for k,v in zip(...)} → {'a':1, 'b':2, 'c':3}.

ch3.title: Dict Comp: With if
ch3.desc: Build dict of even numbers only: {x: x*2 for x in range(10) if x%2==0}. Print it.
ch3.code: d = {x: x * 2 for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0} print(d) # {0:0, 2:4, 4:8, 6:12, 8:16}
guidance: Filter with if: only even x become keys.

ch3.title: Dict Comp: Swap Key-Value
ch3.desc: Given d = {'a':1, 'b':2}, build reversed dict {v: k for k,v in d.items()}. Print it.
guidance: Iterate d.items(); use v as key and k as value.

ch3.title: Dict Comp: From String
ch3.desc: Build dict mapping each character of 'ab' to its index: {c: i for i, c in enumerate('ab')}. Print it.
ch3.code: d = {c: i for i, c in enumerate("ab")} print(d) # {a:0, b:1}
guidance: enumerate('ab') gives (0,'a'), (1,'b').

ch4.title: Define a Class
ch4.desc: Define an empty class named Dog using the class keyword. Then create an instance: d = Dog().
ch4.code: class Dog: pass d = Dog() print(type(d))
guidance: class Dog: defines a class; use pass for an empty body.
Create an instance with Dog().

ch4.title: Create Instance
ch4.desc: Define class Person. Create two instances p1 = Person() and p2 = Person(). Print whether they are the same object (p1 is p2).
ch4.code: class Person: pass p1 = Person() p2 = Person() print(p1 is p2) # False
guidance: Each call to Person() creates a new instance.
p1 is p2 is False (different objects).

ch4.title: Class and type()
ch4.desc: Define class Cat. Create c = Cat() and print type(c). It should show <class '__main__.Cat'>.
ch4.code: class Cat: pass c = Cat() print(type(c))
guidance: type(obj) returns the class of the object.
type(c) is the Cat class.

ch4.title: Dot Access
ch4.desc: Define class Box with no body (pass). After creating b = Box(), assign b.value = 10 and print b.value.
ch4.code: class Box: pass b = Box() b.value = 10 print(b.value) # 10
guidance: You can add attributes to an instance with dot notation: b.value = 10.
Read with b.value.

ch4.title: Multiple Instances
ch4.desc: Define class Counter. Create c1 and c2, set c1.n = 1 and c2.n = 2. Print c1.n and c2.n.
ch4.code: class Counter: pass c1 = Counter() c2 = Counter() c1.n = 1 c2.n = 2 print(c1.n, c2.n) # 1 2
guidance: Each instance has its own attributes; c1.n and c2.n are independent.

ch4.title: Class Name
ch4.desc: Define class Animal. Print Animal.__name__ (the class name as string).
ch4.code: class Animal: pass print(Animal.___) # Animal
guidance: Classes have a __name__ attribute. Fill: __name__.

ch4.title: Instance of Class
ch4.desc: Define class Vehicle. Create v = Vehicle(). Use isinstance(v, Vehicle) and print the result.
ch4.code: class Vehicle: pass v = Vehicle() print(isinstance(v, Vehicle)) # True
guidance: isinstance(obj, Class) returns True if obj is an instance of Class (or subclass).

ch4.title: Empty Class with pass
ch4.desc: In Python a class body cannot be empty. Use 'pass' as a placeholder. Define class Empty with pass and create e = Empty().
ch4.code: class Empty: pass e = Empty() print(e)
guidance: pass is a no-op; it satisfies the syntax for an empty block.

ch4.title: Assign Attribute After Creation
ch4.desc: Create a class Item. Create obj = Item(), then set obj.name = 'apple' and obj.price = 1.5. Print both.
ch4.code: class Item: pass obj = Item() obj.name = "apple" obj.price = 1.5 print(obj.name, obj.price)
guidance: Instance attributes can be added anytime after creation.

ch4.title: Class vs Instance
ch4.desc: Define class C. Create a = C() and b = C(). Print a == b (False; different instances) and type(a) == type(b) (True).
ch4.code: class C: pass a = C() b = C() print(a == b, type(a) == type(b)) # False True
guidance: a and b are different objects so a == b is False.
type(a) and type(b) are both C, so type(a)==type(b) is True.

ch4.title: __init__ Basics
ch4.desc: Define class Greeter with __init__(self, name) that sets self.name = name. Create g = Greeter('Ali') and print g.name.
ch4.code: class Greeter: def __init__(self, name): self.name = name g = Greeter("Ali") print(g.name) # Ali
guidance: __init__ is called when you create an instance; first parameter is self.
Store arguments as self.attr.

ch4.title: self Parameter
ch4.desc: In a method, self refers to the instance. Define class Point with __init__(self, x, y) setting self.x and self.y. Create Point(3, 4) and print p.x, p.y.
ch4.code: class Point: def __init__(self, x, y): self.x = x self.y = y p = Point(3, 4) print(p.x, p.y) # 3 4
guidance: Always list self first in instance methods.
self.x = x assigns to the instance.

ch4.title: __init__ with Default
ch4.desc: Define class Counter with __init__(self, start=0) setting self.count = start. Create c = Counter() and c2 = Counter(10). Print c.count, c2.count.
ch4.code: class Counter: def __init__(self, start=0): self.count = start c = Counter() c2 = Counter(10) print(c.count, c2.count) # 0 10
guidance: Default arguments work in __init__: start=0.
Counter() uses 0; Counter(10) uses 10.

ch4.title: Multiple Attributes in __init__
ch4.desc: Define class Book with __init__(self, title, author). Set both on self. Create b = Book('Python', 'Guido') and print b.title, b.author.
ch4.code: class Book: def __init__(self, title, author): self.title = title self.author = author b = Book("Python", "Guido") print(b.title, b.author)
guidance: Assign each parameter to self.attr in __init__.

ch4.title: __init__ No Return
ch4.desc: __init__ should not return a value (other than None). Define class A with __init__(self) that only does pass. Create a = A().
ch4.code: class A: def __init__(self): pass a = A() print(a)
guidance: __init__ is called for side effects (setting attributes). Returning something else can break instance creation.

ch4.title: self in __init__
ch4.desc: Define class Dog with __init__(self, name). Set self.name = name. Create d = Dog('Rex') and print d.name.
ch4.code: class Dog: def __init__(self, name): self.name = ___ d = Dog("Rex") print(d.name) # Rex
guidance: Use the parameter name: self.name = name. Fill: name.

ch4.title: Optional __init__ Arg
ch4.desc: Define class Config with __init__(self, env='dev'). Set self.env = env. Create Config() and Config('prod'); print both .env.
ch4.code: class Config: def __init__(self, env="dev"): self.env = env c1 = Config() c2 = Config("prod") print(c1.env, c2.env) # dev prod
guidance: Default env='dev'; Config() gives dev, Config('prod') gives prod.

ch4.title: __init__ and Validation
ch4.desc: Define class Age with __init__(self, n). Set self.years = n only if n >= 0 else 0. Create Age(25) and Age(-1); print .years.
ch4.code: class Age: def __init__(self, n): self.years = n if n >= 0 else 0 a = Age(25) b = Age(-1) print(a.years, b.years) # 25 0
guidance: Use a conditional in __init__ to validate: self.years = n if n >= 0 else 0.

ch4.title: Instance vs Class Attribute
ch4.desc: Define class C with class attribute kind = 'C' and __init__(self, x) setting self.x = x. Create c = C(1). Print c.x and C.kind.
ch4.code: class C: kind = "C" def __init__(self, x): self.x = x c = C(1) print(c.x, C.kind) # 1 C
guidance: Attributes defined on the class are shared; those set in __init__ on self are per-instance.

ch4.title: Class Attribute Access
ch4.desc: Define class Animal with class attribute species = 'unknown'. Print Animal.species. Create a = Animal() and print a.species (same value).
ch4.code: class Animal: species = "unknown" print(Animal.species) a = Animal() print(a.species)
guidance: Instance can read class attribute: a.species looks up to Animal.species if not on a.

ch4.title: Shadowing Class Attr
ch4.desc: Class C has count = 0. In __init__ set self.count = 1. Create c = C(). Print c.count (1) and C.count (0).
ch4.code: class C: count = 0 def __init__(self): self.count = 1 c = C() print(c.count, C.count) # 1 0
guidance: Assigning self.count creates an instance attribute that shadows the class attribute for that instance.

ch4.title: Default Mutable Warning
ch4.desc: Avoid using mutable default in __init__: def __init__(self, items=None): self.items = items if items is not None else []. Create two instances and append to one; other stays empty.
ch4.code: class Bag: def __init__(self, items=None): self.items = items if items is not None else [] b1 = Bag() b2 = Bag() b1.items.append(1) print(b1.items, b2.items) # [1] []
guidance: Using def __init__(self, items=[]): would share one list. Use None and assign [] instead.

ch4.title: hasattr and getattr
ch4.desc: Create class C with self.x = 5. Use hasattr(c, 'x') and getattr(c, 'x'). Print both.
ch4.code: class C: def __init__(self): self.x = 5 c = C() print(hasattr(c, "x"), getattr(c, "x")) # True 5
guidance: hasattr(obj, 'name') checks if attribute exists; getattr(obj, 'name') gets value.

ch4.title: setattr
ch4.desc: Define class Empty with pass. Create e = Empty(), then setattr(e, 'value', 42) and print e.value.
ch4.code: class Empty: pass e = Empty() setattr(e, "value", 42) print(e.value) # 42
guidance: setattr(obj, 'name', value) is like obj.name = value when the name is in a variable.

ch4.title: Instance Method
ch4.desc: Define class Greeter with def greet(self): return 'Hello'. Create g = Greeter() and print g.greet().
ch4.code: class Greeter: def greet(self): return "Hello" g = Greeter() print(g.greet()) # Hello
guidance: Instance methods take self as first parameter. Call with obj.method().

ch4.title: Method Using self
ch4.desc: Define class Adder with __init__(self, n) and method add(self, x) returning self.n + x. Create a = Adder(10), print a.add(5).
ch4.code: class Adder: def __init__(self, n): self.n = n def add(self, x): return self.n + x a = Adder(10) print(a.add(5)) # 15
guidance: Methods can read self.n and other instance attributes.

ch4.title: @classmethod
ch4.desc: Define class C with @classmethod def get_name(cls): return cls.__name__. Create C and print C.get_name().
ch4.code: class C: @classmethod def get_name(cls): return cls.__name__ print(C.get_name()) # C
guidance: @classmethod receives cls (the class) as first argument. Call as C.get_name().

ch4.title: @staticmethod
ch4.desc: Define class Math with @staticmethod def square(x): return x*x. Print Math.square(5).
ch4.code: class Math: @staticmethod def square(x): return x * x print(Math.square(5)) # 25
guidance: @staticmethod has no self or cls; it is just a function in the class namespace.

ch4.title: classmethod from Instance
ch4.desc: Class C has @classmethod def info(cls): return cls.__name__. Create c = C(). Call c.info() and print (works; cls is C).
ch4.code: class C: @classmethod def info(cls): return cls.__name__ c = C() print(c.info()) # C
guidance: Calling c.info() still passes C as cls; classmethods work from instances too.

ch4.title: Method Calling Method
ch4.desc: Define class Calc with add(self, a, b) returning a+b and double_add(self, a, b) returning self.add(a,b)*2. Create c = Calc(), print c.double_add(1, 2).
ch4.code: class Calc: def add(self, a, b): return a + b def double_add(self, a, b): return self.add(a, b) * 2 c = Calc() print(c.double_add(1, 2)) # 6
guidance: Use self.add(a, b) to call another method from the same class.

ch4.title: staticmethod No self
ch4.desc: Define class Utils with @staticmethod def is_even(n): return n % 2 == 0. Print Utils.is_even(4) and Utils.is_even(5).
ch4.code: class Utils: @staticmethod def is_even(n): return n % 2 == 0 print(Utils.is_even(4), Utils.is_even(5)) # True False
guidance: Static methods don't receive self; they're like module-level functions grouped in the class.

ch4.title: Factory classmethod
ch4.desc: Define class Point with __init__(self, x, y) and @classmethod from_tuple(cls, t): return cls(t[0], t[1]). Create p = Point.from_tuple((2, 3)); print p.x, p.y.
ch4.code: class Point: def __init__(self, x, y): self.x, self.y = x, y @classmethod def from_tuple(cls, t): return cls(t[0], t[1]) p = Point.from_tuple((2, 3)) print(p.x, p.y) # 2 3
guidance: from_tuple is an alternative constructor; cls(t[0], t[1]) creates a new instance.

ch4.title: Simple Inheritance
ch4.desc: Define class Animal with pass. Define class Dog(Animal) with pass. Create d = Dog(). Print isinstance(d, Dog) and isinstance(d, Animal).
ch4.code: class Animal: pass class Dog(Animal): pass d = Dog() print(isinstance(d, Dog), isinstance(d, Animal)) # True True
guidance: Dog(Animal) means Dog inherits from Animal. d is instance of both Dog and Animal.

ch4.title: Override Method
ch4.desc: Class Animal has def speak(self): return '?'. Class Dog(Animal) overrides with return 'woof'. Create d = Dog(), print d.speak().
ch4.code: class Animal: def speak(self): return "?" class Dog(Animal): def speak(self): return "woof" d = Dog() print(d.speak()) # woof
guidance: Subclass can redefine a method; Dog.speak overrides Animal.speak.

ch4.title: super() Call Parent
ch4.desc: Class A has greet(self): return 'A'. Class B(A) has greet(self): return super().greet() + 'B'. Create b = B(), print b.greet().
ch4.code: class A: def greet(self): return "A" class B(A): def greet(self): return super().greet() + "B" b = B() print(b.greet()) # AB
guidance: super().greet() calls the parent's greet(); then add 'B'.

ch4.title: super() in __init__
ch4.desc: Class Person has __init__(self, name): self.name = name. Class Employee(Person) has __init__(self, name, id): super().__init__(name); self.id = id. Create e = Employee('Jo', 1); print e.name, e.id.
ch4.code: class Person: def __init__(self, name): self.name = name class Employee(Person): def __init__(self, name, id): super().__init__(name) self.id = id e = Employee("Jo", 1) print(e.name, e.id) # Jo 1
guidance: Call super().__init__(name) first so self.name is set; then set self.id.

ch4.title: Inherited Attribute
ch4.desc: Class A has __init__(self): self.x = 1. Class B(A) has pass. Create b = B(). B has no __init__ so A's is used. Print b.x.
ch4.code: class A: def __init__(self): self.x = 1 class B(A): pass b = B() print(b.x) # 1
guidance: B() calls A.__init__ (inherited); so b.x is set to 1.

ch4.title: issubclass
ch4.desc: Define class Base and class Derived(Base). Print issubclass(Derived, Base) and issubclass(Base, Derived).
ch4.code: class Base: pass class Derived(Base): pass print(issubclass(Derived, Base), issubclass(Base, Derived)) # True False
guidance: issubclass(Derived, Base) is True; Base is not a subclass of Derived.

ch4.title: Multiple Inheritance Intro
ch4.desc: Define class A: pass and class B: pass. Define class C(A, B): pass. Create c = C(). Print C.__bases__ (tuple of base classes).
ch4.code: class A: pass class B: pass class C(A, B): pass c = C() print(C.__bases__) # (A, B)
guidance: class C(A, B): inherits from both. __bases__ gives (A, B).

ch4.title: Override and Extend
ch4.desc: Class A has run(self): return 1. Class B(A) has run(self): return super().run() + 2. Create B(), print b.run().
ch4.code: class A: def run(self): return 1 class B(A): def run(self): return super().run() + 2 b = B() print(b.run()) # 3
guidance: super().run() returns 1; add 2 gives 3.

ch4.title: Child Without __init__
ch4.desc: Class Parent has __init__(self, x): self.x = x. Class Child(Parent): pass. Create c = Child(5). Parent's __init__ is used. Print c.x.
ch4.code: class Parent: def __init__(self, x): self.x = x class Child(Parent): pass c = Child(5) print(c.x) # 5
guidance: Child has no __init__, so Parent.__init__ is called when Child(5) is used.

ch4.title: Override __init__ with super
ch4.desc: Class Animal has __init__(self, name): self.name = name. Class Dog(Animal) has __init__(self, name, breed): super().__init__(name); self.breed = breed. Create Dog('Rex', 'Lab'); print name and breed.
ch4.code: class Animal: def __init__(self, name): self.name = name class Dog(Animal): def __init__(self, name, breed): super().__init__(name) self.breed = breed d = Dog("Rex", "Lab") print(d.name, d.breed) # Rex Lab
guidance: Always call super().__init__(name) in Dog before setting Dog-specific attributes.

ch4.title: Private Convention _name
ch4.desc: By convention, a single leading underscore _ means 'internal'. Define class C with __init__(self): self._x = 1. Create c = C(), print c._x (still accessible).
ch4.code: class C: def __init__(self): self._x = 1 c = C() print(c._x) # 1
guidance: _x is a hint to developers; Python does not enforce it. It is still readable and writable.

ch4.title: Name Mangling __name
ch4.desc: Double underscore __ triggers name mangling: __x becomes _C__x inside class C. Define class C with self.__val = 10. Access via c._C__val or define a getter.
ch4.code: class C: def __init__(self): self.__val = 10 def get_val(self): return self.__val c = C() print(c.get_val()) # 10
guidance: __val is mangled to _C__val. Use a method get_val() to expose it.

ch4.title: @property Getter
ch4.desc: Define class Circle with __init__(self, r): self._r = r and @property def radius(self): return self._r. Create c = Circle(5); print c.radius (no parentheses).
ch4.code: class Circle: def __init__(self, r): self._r = r @property def radius(self): return self._r c = Circle(5) print(c.radius) # 5
guidance: @property makes radius() callable as an attribute: c.radius, not c.radius().

ch4.title: Property Setter
ch4.desc: Class C has _x = 0, @property def x(self): return self._x, @x.setter def x(self, v): self._x = max(0, v). Create c = C(); c.x = 5; c.x = -1; print c.x.
ch4.code: class C: _x = 0 @property def x(self): return self._x @x.setter def x(self, v): self._x = max(0, v) c = C() c.x = 5 c.x = -1 print(c.x) # 0
guidance: Setter ensures _x is never negative; c.x = -1 stores 0 via max(0, v).

ch4.title: Read-Only Property
ch4.desc: Define class ReadOnly with __init__(self, v): self._v = v and @property def value(self): return self._v (no setter). Create r = ReadOnly(42); print r.value. Assigning r.value = 0 would raise AttributeError.
ch4.code: class ReadOnly: def __init__(self, v): self._v = v @property def value(self): return self._v r = ReadOnly(42) print(r.value) # 42
guidance: Property without setter is read-only; r.value = 0 would error.

ch4.title: __str__
ch4.desc: Define class Person with __init__(self, name) and __str__(self): return self.name. Create p = Person('Ali'). print(p) uses __str__; print str(p).
ch4.code: class Person: def __init__(self, name): self.name = name def __str__(self): return self.name p = Person("Ali") print(p) # Ali
guidance: __str__ is used by print() and str(); return a human-readable string.

ch4.title: __repr__
ch4.desc: Define class Point with __init__(self, x, y) and __repr__(self): return 'Point(%s, %s)' % (self.x, self.y). Create Point(1, 2); repr(p) or echo in REPL uses __repr__.
ch4.code: class Point: def __init__(self, x, y): self.x, self.y = x, y def __repr__(self): return "Point(%s, %s)" % (self.x, self.y) p = Point(1, 2) print(repr(p)) # Point(1, 2)
guidance: __repr__ should be unambiguous; often like constructor call. Used by repr() and REPL.

ch4.title: __eq__
ch4.desc: Define class Box with __init__(self, v) and __eq__(self, other): return isinstance(other, Box) and self.v == other.v. Create Box(1) and Box(1); print Box(1) == Box(1).
ch4.code: class Box: def __init__(self, v): self.v = v def __eq__(self, other): return isinstance(other, Box) and self.v == other.v print(Box(1) == Box(1)) # True
guidance: __eq__ defines ==. Check type with isinstance; then compare attributes.

ch4.title: Same Method Name, Different Classes
ch4.desc: Define class Dog with speak(self): return 'woof'. Define class Cat with speak(self): return 'meow'. Create d = Dog(), c = Cat(); print d.speak(), c.speak().
ch4.code: class Dog: def speak(self): return "woof" class Cat: def speak(self): return "meow" d, c = Dog(), Cat() print(d.speak(), c.speak()) # woof meow
guidance: Polymorphism: same method name speak, different behavior per class.

ch4.title: Loop Over Different Types
ch4.desc: Dog and Cat both have speak(). Put instances in a list: [Dog(), Cat()]. Loop and print each .speak().
ch4.code: class Dog: def speak(self): return "woof" class Cat: def speak(self): return "meow" for obj in [Dog(), Cat()]: print(obj.speak()) # woof then meow
guidance: One loop, one call obj.speak(); each object responds with its own implementation.

ch4.title: Polymorphic Function
ch4.desc: Write def make_sound(animal): return animal.speak(). Call with Dog() and Cat(); print both results.
ch4.code: class Dog: def speak(self): return "woof" class Cat: def speak(self): return "meow" def make_sound(animal): return animal.speak() print(make_sound(Dog()), make_sound(Cat())) # woof meow
guidance: make_sound doesn't care about the concrete type; it only needs .speak().

ch4.title: Override and Call Same Name
ch4.desc: Class Animal has speak(self): return '?'. Dog(Animal) overrides with 'woof'. Create a = Dog(); print a.speak() (uses Dog's version).
ch4.code: class Animal: def speak(self): return "?" class Dog(Animal): def speak(self): return "woof" a = Dog() print(a.speak()) # woof
guidance: Variable a is a Dog; a.speak() resolves to Dog.speak (override).

ch4.title: Duck Typing
ch4.desc: Duck typing: if it has .quack(), use it. Define class Duck with quack(self): return 'quack'. Define class Person with quack(self): return 'fake quack'. Write def say_it(x): return x.quack(). Call with Duck() and Person().
ch4.code: class Duck: def quack(self): return "quack" class Person: def quack(self): return "fake quack" def say_it(x): return x.quack() print(say_it(Duck()), say_it(Person())) # quack fake quack
guidance: No common base class; Python uses duck typing: same method name, different classes.

ch4.title: Operator Overloading __add__
ch4.desc: Define class Vector with __init__(self, x, y) and __add__(self, other): return Vector(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y). Create v1 = Vector(1,0), v2 = Vector(0,1); print (v1+v2).x, (v1+v2).y.
ch4.code: class Vector: def __init__(self, x, y): self.x, self.y = x, y def __add__(self, other): return Vector(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y) v1, v2 = Vector(1, 0), Vector(0, 1) v = v1 + v2 print(v.x, v.y) # 1 1
guidance: __add__ is called for +; return a new Vector. Polymorphism: + means different things for int vs Vector.

ch4.title: Polymorphism with len()
ch4.desc: Define class MyList with __init__(self, data): self.data = data and __len__(self): return len(self.data). Create m = MyList([1,2,3]); print len(m).
ch4.code: class MyList: def __init__(self, data): self.data = data def __len__(self): return len(self.data) m = MyList([1, 2, 3]) print(len(m)) # 3
guidance: Built-in len() calls __len__; your class can plug into the same interface.

ch4.title: Common Interface
ch4.desc: Define abstract interface: class Shape with area(self): pass. Rectangle(Shape) and Circle(Shape) override area(). Put [Rectangle(2,3), Circle(1)] in list; loop and print each .area().
ch4.code: class Shape: def area(self): pass class Rectangle(Shape): def __init__(self, w, h): self.w, self.h = w, h def area(self): return self.w * self.h class Circle(Shape): def __init__(self, r): self.r = r def area(self): return 3.14 * self.r * self.r for s in [Rectangle(2,3), Circle(1)]: print(s.area())
guidance: Same .area() call; Rectangle and Circle behave differently (polymorphism).

ch4.title: Method Resolution Order
ch4.desc: Class A: def go(self): return 'A'. Class B(A): def go(self): return 'B'. Class C(A): def go(self): return 'C'. Class D(B, C): pass. Create d = D(); print d.go(). Which parent wins? (MRO: D, B, C, A)
ch4.code: class A: def go(self): return "A" class B(A): def go(self): return "B" class C(A): def go(self): return "C" class D(B, C): pass d = D() print(d.go()) # B
guidance: MRO: D -> B -> C -> A. First definition of go is in B, so d.go() returns 'B'.

ch4.title: Polymorphic __getitem__
ch4.desc: Define class Seq with __init__(self, data): self.data = data and __getitem__(self, i): return self.data[i]. Create s = Seq([10,20,30]); print s[1]. Now s[1] works like a list.
ch4.code: class Seq: def __init__(self, data): self.data = data def __getitem__(self, i): return self.data[i] s = Seq([10, 20, 30]) print(s[1]) # 20
guidance: __getitem__ makes obj[i] work; same interface as list indexing (polymorphism).

ch4.title: Abstract Idea: Base with pass
ch4.desc: Define class Animal with def speak(self): pass (no implementation). Subclass Dog(Animal) with speak(self): return 'woof'. Create d = Dog(); print d.speak().
ch4.code: class Animal: def speak(self): pass class Dog(Animal): def speak(self): return "woof" d = Dog() print(d.speak()) # woof
guidance: Animal.speak does nothing; subclasses provide real implementation. Base is 'abstract' in idea.

ch4.title: ABC: Import and Inherit
ch4.desc: from abc import ABC, abstractmethod. Define class Shape(ABC) with @abstractmethod def area(self): pass. Subclass Rectangle(Shape) with area(self): return 10. Create r = Rectangle(); print r.area().
ch4.code: from abc import ABC, abstractmethod class Shape(ABC): @abstractmethod def area(self): pass class Rectangle(Shape): def area(self): return 10 r = Rectangle() print(r.area()) # 10
guidance: ABC = Abstract Base Class. You cannot instantiate Shape(); only concrete subclasses like Rectangle.

ch4.title: Cannot Instantiate ABC
ch4.desc: Class Shape(ABC) has @abstractmethod def area(self): pass. Try shape = Shape() — it raises TypeError. Only concrete subclasses that implement area() can be instantiated.
ch4.code: from abc import ABC, abstractmethod class Shape(ABC): @abstractmethod def area(self): pass # Shape() TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class
guidance: Abstract methods force subclasses to implement them; Shape() is forbidden.

ch4.title: Multiple Abstract Methods
ch4.desc: Define class Worker(ABC) with @abstractmethod def work(self): pass and @abstractmethod def rest(self): pass. Class Programmer(Worker) implements both. Create p = Programmer(), call p.work() and p.rest().
ch4.code: from abc import ABC, abstractmethod class Worker(ABC): @abstractmethod def work(self): pass @abstractmethod def rest(self): pass class Programmer(Worker): def work(self): return "coding" def rest(self): return "coffee" p = Programmer() print(p.work(), p.rest()) # coding coffee
guidance: All abstract methods must be implemented before the subclass can be instantiated.

ch4.title: Abstract Property
ch4.desc: Class Base(ABC) has @abstractmethod def value(self): pass. Subclass Concrete(Base) has def value(self): return 42. Create c = Concrete(); print c.value().
ch4.code: from abc import ABC, abstractmethod class Base(ABC): @abstractmethod def value(self): pass class Concrete(Base): def value(self): return 42 c = Concrete() print(c.value()) # 42
guidance: Abstract method can be a getter; subclasses must implement value().

ch4.title: Concrete + Abstract in One Class
ch4.desc: Class Animal(ABC) has @abstractmethod speak(self): pass and concrete method name(self): return self.__class__.__name__. Dog(Animal) implements speak. Create d = Dog(); print d.name(), d.speak().
ch4.code: from abc import ABC, abstractmethod class Animal(ABC): @abstractmethod def speak(self): pass def name(self): return self.__class__.__name__ class Dog(Animal): def speak(self): return "woof" d = Dog() print(d.name(), d.speak()) # Dog woof
guidance: Abstract class can have both abstract and concrete methods; name() is shared.

ch4.title: Abstract Class as Type Hint
ch4.desc: Define def process(s: Shape): return s.area(). Shape is ABC. Call process(Rectangle(2,3)) and process(Circle(1)). Polymorphism: same function, different shapes.
ch4.code: from abc import ABC, abstractmethod class Shape(ABC): @abstractmethod def area(self): pass class Rectangle(Shape): def __init__(self,w,h): self.w,self.h = w,h def area(self): return self.w*self.h class Circle(Shape): def __init__(self,r): self.r = r def area(self): return 3.14*self.r*self.r def process(s): return s.area() print(process(Rectangle(2,3)), process(Circle(1))) # 6 3.14...
guidance: process(s) works for any Shape; abstraction defines the contract.

ch4.title: Subclass Without Implementing
ch4.desc: Shape(ABC) has @abstractmethod area(self): pass. Class Incomplete(Shape): pass. Try Incomplete() — TypeError: must implement area.
ch4.code: from abc import ABC, abstractmethod class Shape(ABC): @abstractmethod def area(self): pass class Incomplete(Shape): pass # Incomplete() TypeError
guidance: Subclass must implement all abstract methods; Incomplete() is still abstract.

ch4.title: ABC with __init__
ch4.desc: Abstract class Vehicle(ABC) has __init__(self, name): self.name = name and @abstractmethod def start(self): pass. Car(Vehicle) calls super().__init__(name) and implements start(). Create c = Car('Tesla'); print c.name, c.start().
ch4.code: from abc import ABC, abstractmethod class Vehicle(ABC): def __init__(self, name): self.name = name @abstractmethod def start(self): pass class Car(Vehicle): def start(self): return "running" c = Car("Tesla") print(c.name, c.start()) # Tesla running
guidance: Abstract class can have __init__; Car(name) calls super().__init__(name) then sets name.

ch4.title: Registering a Virtual Subclass
ch4.desc: Shape(ABC) with @abstractmethod area(self): pass. Class MyShape has def area(self): return 99. Register: Shape.register(MyShape). Now isinstance(MyShape(), Shape) is True. Create m = MyShape(); print m.area().
ch4.code: from abc import ABC, abstractmethod class Shape(ABC): @abstractmethod def area(self): pass class MyShape: def area(self): return 99 Shape.register(MyShape) m = MyShape() print(m.area(), isinstance(m, Shape)) # 99 True
guidance: register() makes MyShape a virtual subclass of Shape without inheriting; isinstance still works.

ch5.title: Library Management System
ch5.desc: Create a Library class with a list of books. Implement display_books(), lend_book(book_name, borrower), and return_book(book_name). Track which books are currently lent out and handle the case when a book is already lent.
guidance: Use a list for available books and a dict (book -> borrower) for lent books.
In lend_book check if the book is in the list and not already lent; then move it to lent tracking.
In return_book remove from lent and add back to available list.
ch5.solutionMethod: Encapsulate book list and a lent dict. display_books shows each book and optionally '(lent to X)'. lend_book validates presence and not already lent; return_book removes from lent.

ch5.title: Employee Payroll with Inheritance
ch5.desc: Create a base class Employee with name. Subclasses: SalariedEmployee(salary per month) and HourlyEmployee(hourly_rate, hours_worked). Each has calculate_pay() returning the appropriate amount. Create one of each and print their pay.
guidance: Base Employee can have __init__(self, name).
SalariedEmployee.__init__(self, name, salary); calculate_pay returns salary.
HourlyEmployee.__init__(self, name, hourly_rate, hours_worked); calculate_pay returns hourly_rate * hours_worked.
ch5.solutionMethod: Inherit from Employee; call super().__init__(name) in subclasses. Override calculate_pay() in each subclass with the correct formula.

ch5.title: Banking System
ch5.desc: BankAccount with account_holder and private balance. Implement deposit(amount), withdraw(amount) (no overdraft), get_balance(). Keep a transaction_history list and log every deposit and withdrawal.
guidance: Use a single leading underscore for 'private' balance, e.g. self._balance.
Append a string or dict to transaction_history in deposit and withdraw.
In withdraw, only deduct if amount <= self._balance.
ch5.solutionMethod: Encapsulate _balance and transaction_history. Every deposit/withdraw updates balance and appends to history; withdraw checks balance first to prevent overdraft.

ch5.title: Shape Area Calculator
ch5.desc: Use the abc module. Abstract class Shape with abstract method area(). Implement Circle(radius) and Rectangle(width, height). You must not be able to instantiate Shape. Create a circle and a rectangle and print their areas.
guidance: from abc import ABC, abstractmethod; class Shape(ABC): with @abstractmethod def area(self): pass.
Circle and Rectangle inherit from Shape and implement area() (pi*r*r and width*height).
ch5.solutionMethod: Shape(ABC) with @abstractmethod area(). Concrete classes Circle and Rectangle implement area() with the correct formulas. Instantiating Shape raises TypeError.

ch5.title: Magic Method Shopping Cart
ch5.desc: Item(name, price). ShoppingCart holds a list of Item. Implement __len__ (number of items) and __str__ (formatted receipt with each item and total at the end). Create a cart, add items, print(len(cart)) and print(cart).
guidance: Item is a simple class with name and price.
ShoppingCart has a list; __len__ returns len(self.items); __str__ builds a string with each 'name - price' and 'Total: ...'.
ch5.solutionMethod: Store items in a list. __len__ delegates to len(self.items). __str__ iterates items, formats name and price, then appends total and returns joined string.

ch5.title: Student Grade Tracker
ch5.desc: Class Student(name). Method add_grade(subject, score). Method get_average(subject) returning average for that subject, or overall average if subject is None. Method get_grades() returning a dict of subject -> list of scores.
guidance: Use a dict mapping subject to list of scores: self._grades = {}.
add_grade: append to self._grades.setdefault(subject, []).
get_average(subject): if subject given, average that list; else average all scores.
ch5.solutionMethod: Store grades as dict of subject -> list of scores. get_average filters by subject or flattens all; return sum/len with guard for empty list.

ch5.title: Vehicle Hierarchy
ch5.desc: Abstract Vehicle(ABC) with start() and stop() abstract. Car and Bike inherit and implement both. Each has a name. Create one Car and one Bike, call start() and stop() and print a short message from each.
guidance: Vehicle has @abstractmethod start(self) and stop(self).
Car and Bike __init__(self, name); start/stop can return or print a message.
ch5.solutionMethod: Abstract Vehicle with two abstract methods. Car and Bike implement both and use self.name in their messages.

ch5.title: Notification System — Polymorphism
ch5.desc: Create a base class Notifier with __init__(self, label) storing self.label, and a send(self, message) method that prints '[label]: message'. Create three subclasses — EmailNotifier(email), SMSNotifier(phone), PushNotifier(device_id) — each calls super().__init__() with an appropriate label string and overrides send() to print a channel-specific formatted message. Store one instance of each in a list and loop through calling send() with the same alert message on all three.
guidance: Notifier.__init__(self, label): self.label = label. send(self, message): print '[' + self.label + '] ' + message. This is the default that subclasses override.
EmailNotifier.__init__(self, email): call super().__init__('Email'); self.email = email. Override send() to print 'Email to {email}: {message}'.
SMSNotifier and PushNotifier follow the same pattern — super().__init__('SMS') or 'Push', store their own attribute (phone or device_id), override send() with a matching format.
Create one instance of each in a list. Loop with 'for n in notifiers: n.send(msg)' — Python calls the correct send() per type automatically. This is polymorphism.
ch5.solutionMethod: Base class Notifier defines the default send() behaviour. Each subclass calls super().__init__() with its own label, stores a unique contact attribute, and overrides send() with a channel-specific format. The for loop over the list is classic polymorphism — the same line n.send() produces different output depending on the actual runtime type of n.

ch5.title: Stack Class
ch5.desc: Class Stack with push(item), pop() (return and remove top; return None if empty), peek() (return top without removing), and is_empty(). Use a list to store elements.
guidance: Use self._items = []. push appends; pop pops if non-empty else None; peek returns last element; is_empty returns len == 0.
ch5.solutionMethod: List as underlying storage. push appends; pop uses list.pop() with guard for empty; peek returns last element; is_empty checks length.

ch5.title: Hospital Patient Registry — @classmethod & @staticmethod
ch5.desc: Build a Patient class with name, age, and ward as instance attributes. Add a class variable _registry = [] to track all admitted patients. Implement @classmethod admit(cls, name, age, ward) that creates a Patient, appends it to _registry, and returns it. Implement @classmethod get_by_ward(cls, ward) returning a list of matching patients. Implement @classmethod total_count(cls) returning the number of admitted patients. Implement @staticmethod is_adult(age) returning True if age >= 18. Admit 3 patients, print the total count, then for each ICU patient print their name and whether they are an adult.
guidance: Class variable: _registry = [] placed directly under 'class Patient:' — not inside __init__. This list is shared across all instances.
@classmethod admit(cls, name, age, ward): p = cls(name, age, ward); cls._registry.append(p); return p. Using cls() instead of Patient() means subclasses also work.
@classmethod get_by_ward(cls, ward): return [p for p in cls._registry if p.ward == ward].
@classmethod total_count(cls): return len(cls._registry).
@staticmethod is_adult(age): return age >= 18. No self or cls — it works on any plain value. Call as Patient.is_adult(p.age).
ch5.solutionMethod: @classmethod admit() is an alternative constructor that also registers every new patient in the shared _registry. @classmethod get_by_ward() and total_count() query that shared list using cls — no instance needed. @staticmethod is_adult() is a pure utility function: it takes a plain age value, makes a decision, and returns True/False — no cls or self involved at all.

ch5.title: Online Order System — Composition
ch5.desc: Build two classes. Product(name, price, stock) is a plain data class. Order(order_id) holds a private _items list of (Product, quantity) tuples. Implement add_item(product, quantity) — only add if quantity does not exceed product.stock, otherwise print an error message. Implement calculate_total() returning the sum of price × quantity for all items. Implement get_summary() returning a formatted multi-line string: a header line with the order ID, one line per item showing name, quantity, and line total, then a final Total line. Create 2 products, one order, add items (include one attempt that exceeds stock), and print the summary.
guidance: Product is a plain data class: __init__(self, name, price, stock) with self.name, self.price, self.stock.
Order: self.order_id and self._items = [] in __init__. Each element of _items is a tuple: (product_object, quantity).
add_item(product, quantity): if quantity > product.stock: print 'Not enough stock for ' + product.name; return. Else: self._items.append((product, quantity)).
calculate_total(): return sum(p.price * qty for p, qty in self._items).
get_summary(): build a list of strings — start with 'Order #' + order_id, loop _items for item lines, append 'Total: $...' at end, return '\n'.join(lines).
ch5.solutionMethod: This is a Composition ('has-a') design: an Order HAS Product objects stored in _items — it does not inherit from Product. Each element is a (Product, quantity) tuple keeping both values paired. add_item validates stock before appending. calculate_total uses a generator expression over the tuples. get_summary builds a list of formatted lines and joins them at the end with newline.

ch5.title: University System — 3-level Inheritance
ch5.desc: Build a 3-level inheritance chain. Person(name, age) with get_info() returning 'Name: {name}, Age: {age}'. Student(Person) adds student_id and a private _grades dict; override get_info() to extend the parent's string; add add_grade(course, grade) to store a grade. GradStudent(Student) adds research_topic and a private _papers list; override get_info() to extend Student's string; add publish_paper(title) to store paper titles. Every level must call super().__init__() passing the required arguments upward. Create a GradStudent, add a grade, publish a paper, and print get_info() along with the grades and papers.
guidance: Person.__init__(self, name, age): self.name = name; self.age = age. get_info(): return 'Name: ' + self.name + ', Age: ' + str(self.age).

Student(Person).__init__(self, name, age, student_id): super().__init__(name, age); self.student_id = student_id; self._grades = {}. get_info(): return super().get_info() + ', ID: ' + self.student_id.
add_grade(course, grade): self._grades[course] = grade — stores a dict of course to grade.
GradStudent(Student).__init__(self, name, age, student_id, research_topic): super().__init__(name, age, student_id); self.research_topic = research_topic; self._papers = [].
publish_paper(title): self._papers.append(title). get_info(): return super().get_info() + ', Research: ' + self.research_topic. Create: gs = GradStudent('Alice', 26, 'G101', 'Machine Learning').
ch5.solutionMethod: Each class adds its own attributes in __init__ and passes parent-required arguments upward via super().__init__(). get_info() at each level prepends the parent's output using super().get_info() — this chains through all three levels so GradStudent.get_info() produces a combined string with all three levels of info. The private _grades and _papers demonstrate encapsulation alongside inheritance.
